title: FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting
one_liner: A time-series model that works at any sampling rate by learning continuous time instead of discrete time steps.
lead: Time-series forecasting (predicting the next values in a sequence) usually trains on data collected at one fixed rate—say, daily observations. If new data arrives at a different rate (hourly or weekly), the trained model breaks. FlowState learns to think of time as continuous rather than as a fixed grid, so it can naturally handle data at any rate without retraining.

paras: Today's time-series models work like this: take data sampled at one fixed rate (say, a temperature reading every hour), train on it, then when new data arrives at a different rate (every 30 minutes or every day), the model fails. It has learned the rhythm of the original grid.

A beginner might try retraining on the new rate, but that is slow and wasteful. Or they might try to resample (stretch or compress the data), but that introduces artifacts and loses information. The core problem is that models bake in the assumption that time is chopped into uniform pieces.

callout.html: FlowState learns that time flows continuously, not in chunks, so the same model handles any sampling rate.

steps.text: SSM reads the time-series and learns a latent state (a compressed representation) as a smooth function of continuous time, not discrete steps.
Functional basis decoder expresses the time series as a weighted sum of smooth basis functions (like sine waves or polynomials), each valid across all times.
To forecast at a new sampling rate, evaluate the basis functions at the new time points; no retraining needed.
The model can forecast any distance into the future (5 steps or 100 steps) without retraining because the basis functions are continuous.
By learning in continuous time, the model is smaller and trains faster than models that must memorize every discrete time step.

paras: Instead of learning a function of discrete time steps, FlowState learns a function of continuous time. The object being changed is the time representation: from a fixed grid to a continuous variable.

hidden.name: Sampling-rate equivariance
paras: Equivariance is a formal name for a symmetry: the output transforms predictably when the input transforms. In FlowState, if you resample the input data at half the rate (take every other point) or double the rate (interpolate new points), the model's predictions transform by the same factor and remain valid. This is not automatic; it is built into how the model thinks about time.

The paper measures this by testing the trained model on datasets at sampling rates it has never seen before, checking that forecasts remain accurate. A model that learned discrete time steps would fail; FlowState succeeds because it learned the continuous skeleton underneath.

heat.caption: Darker means the property holds strongly; check marks highlight equivariance working as promised.

reads.html: The model works the same way no matter what rate the time series arrives at, because it learned time as continuous, not as a rigid grid.
The functional basis representation is equivariant to sampling-rate transformations; the state space model encoder discovers this invariance in the data.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: two layers, one vision
paras: Any smooth time series can be written as a sum of simpler smooth pieces (basis functions like sine waves or Chebyshev polynomials). If you learn the coefficients of those pieces, you can regenerate the series at any resolution by evaluating the pieces at any time points you choose.

The SSM encoder compresses the observed time series into latent states that represent the coefficients of the basis functions. A state space model is a way to process sequences efficiently by maintaining a hidden state and updating it as you read each value; this lets the encoder learn from data sampled at any rate, because it does not assume a fixed grid.

The functional basis decoder reconstructs the time series from those learned coefficients. Because the basis functions are themselves continuous, forecasting at a new rate is just evaluating them at new times. No retraining, no discretization artifacts.

items.html: If the time series contains high-frequency changes (rapid oscillations), but you choose too few basis functions, the model misses details and forecasts poorly. The fix: use more basis functions, at the cost of more memory and computation.

Forecasting far into the future works only if the basis functions remain valid at those times. If the system changes its behavior over very long horizons, the stationary assumption breaks and predictions drift.
If the underlying signal evolves over time (e.g., a sensor drifts), the basis functions learned on early data become stale. The model assumes the signal is stable in structure.
Choose enough basis functions to capture the data's details, train on representative examples across time ranges, and test on unseen rates before deploying.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic time series (e.g., a mixture of sine waves and noise) and sample it at an initial rate (hourly). Train FlowState on this data. Then subsample or oversample the time grid (test at 30-minute or 4-hour intervals), and verify that the model's forecast error stays roughly constant. Compare against a baseline model trained only on hourly data, which should fail on new rates.
demo.closing: If equivariance_hold is near 1.0 for multiple unseen rates, the model truly learned continuous time.
